issues.legal_issue: A transfer of a corporate debtor’s property is an avoidable preference when it benefits a creditor, surety, or guarantor for an antecedent liability, improves that person’s position in insolvency distribution, occurs within the applicable look-back period, and is not within a statutory exclusion.
material_facts: During the corporate insolvency resolution process, the debtor mortgaged its unencumbered land to secure facilities granted to its holding company.
The holding company was a related party, an operational creditor, and a surety of the debtor, which owed it antecedent liabilities.
The mortgages improved the holding company’s position and reduced the assets available to the debtor’s other creditors and stakeholders.
The challenged mortgages were created or renewed within the applicable period before insolvency commenced.
issues.conclusion: The transactions involving the six properties were preferential under Section 43 and were properly avoided; the directions discharging the security interests and restoring the properties to the corporate debtor were upheld.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 43(1), 43(2)(a) and (b), and 43(4) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, a preference is deemed to exist when a transfer of the corporate debtor’s property benefits a creditor, surety, or guarantor on account of an antecedent liability owed by the debtor and places that person in a better position than distribution under Section 53 would. The applicable period is two years for a related party other than an employee and one year for another person. If the requirements are met and no Section 43(3) exclusion applies, intent to prefer is not required. The resolution professional may seek avoidance during the resolution process under Section 25(2)(j), and the Adjudicating Authority may grant relief under Section 44. The Court applied the statutory deeming principle discussed in Pioneer Urban Land and Infrastructure Ltd. v. Union of India.

rule.if: corporate_insolvency_preference_review and transfer_of_debtor_property and transfer_benefits_creditor_for_antecedent_debtor_liability and improves_insolvency_distribution_position and within_applicable_lookback_period and not ordinary_course_exception_applies and not new_value_exception_applies

predicates.corporate_insolvency_preference_review: A resolution professional or liquidator sought review of a corporate debtor’s transaction for avoidance as a preference in an insolvency proceeding.
predicates.transfer_of_debtor_property: The corporate debtor transferred property or an interest in its property.
predicates.transfer_benefits_creditor_for_anteceden: The transfer benefited a creditor, surety, or guarantor in connection with a liability the corporate debtor already owed.
predicates.improves_insolvency_distribution_positio: The transfer placed the beneficiary in a better position than that person would have occupied in the distribution of the debtor’s assets.
predicates.within_applicable_lookback_period: The transfer occurred within the applicable period preceding insolvency, assessed by whether the beneficiary was related to the corporate debtor.
predicates.ordinary_course_exception_applies: The transfer was made in the ordinary course of business or financial affairs of both the corporate debtor and the transferee.
predicates.new_value_exception_applies: The transfer created security in property acquired by the corporate debtor, secured new value, and met the other requirements for that exclusion.

issues.definition: When a debtor-property transfer in an insolvency preference review benefits a creditor, surety, or guarantor for an existing debtor liability, improves that beneficiary’s distribution position, falls within the applicable look-back period, and meets neither stated exclusion, the transfer is an avoidable preference.

issues.legal_issue: The ordinary-course exclusion from preference avoidance applies only when the transfer was made in the ordinary course of business or financial affairs of both the corporate debtor and the transferee.
material_facts: The corporate debtor was established to develop and operate an infrastructure project and related real-estate projects.
It mortgaged substantial unencumbered land to secure its holding company’s borrowing, rather than to fund its own business.
The debtor was under financial stress, had defaulted to creditors, and faced obligations to home buyers.
The lender-transferees conducted lending business, but the mortgages were not part of the debtor’s ordinary business or financial affairs.
issues.conclusion: The word “or” in Section 43(3)(a) was read conjunctively as “and”; the mortgages were not in the ordinary course of the corporate debtor’s business or financial affairs, so the exclusion did not apply.
issues.legal_principle: Section 43(3)(a) excludes a transfer made in the ordinary course of business or financial affairs of the corporate debtor or the transferee. To keep the inquiry focused on the debtor’s conduct and to avoid frustrating Section 43, the Court purposively construed “or” as “and,” requiring the transfer to be ordinary for both. The Court relied on State of Bombay v. R.M.D. Chamarbaugwala and Mazagaon Dock Ltd. v. Commissioner of Income-Tax and Excess Profits Tax for reading “or” as “and” where necessary to reflect legislative intent, and on Downs Distributing Co. Pty Ltd. v. Associated Blue Star Stores Pty Ltd. for the ordinary-course standard: the transaction must form part of the usual, undistinguished flow of business and not arise from a special situation.

predicates.corporate_insolvency_preference_review: A resolution professional or liquidator sought review of a corporate debtor’s transaction for avoidance as a preference in an insolvency proceeding.
predicates.transfer_not_in_ordinary_course_for_both: The transfer was not made in the ordinary course of business or financial affairs of at least one of the corporate debtor and the transferee.

issues.definition: In an insolvency preference review, if a transfer was not ordinary for both the debtor and the transferee, the ordinary-course exclusion is unavailable.

issues.legal_issue: A mortgage released by the mortgagee and subsequently created again is a fresh transfer, even when the same property is mortgaged to the same lender on the release date.
material_facts: Several properties had previously been mortgaged to secure the holding company’s borrowing.
The earlier mortgages were released, after which the corporate debtor executed new mortgage deeds over the properties.
Some new mortgages were executed on the same day as release of the earlier mortgages, and some secured increased facilities.
issues.conclusion: The renewed mortgages were fresh transactions, not continuations of the earlier mortgages, and those made within the applicable look-back period could be treated as preferences.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 43, a preference must be given within the relevant period under Section 43(4). Once a mortgage is released, it ceases to exist; a later mortgage is a fresh transfer and must be assessed as such. The same-property, same-lender, or same-day circumstances do not convert a new mortgage into a continuation of the released mortgage.

rule.if: corporate_insolvency_preference_review and earlier_mortgage_released and debtor_creates_new_mortgage and new_mortgage_within_applicable_lookback_period

predicates.corporate_insolvency_preference_review: A resolution professional or liquidator sought review of a corporate debtor’s transaction for avoidance as a preference in an insolvency proceeding.
predicates.earlier_mortgage_released: The mortgagee released the earlier mortgage over the property.
predicates.debtor_creates_new_mortgage: The corporate debtor created another mortgage over the property after the earlier mortgage was released.
predicates.new_mortgage_within_applicable_lookback_: The newly created mortgage occurred within the applicable period preceding insolvency, assessed by whether its beneficiary was related to the corporate debtor.

issues.definition: When an earlier mortgage has been released and the debtor creates another mortgage within the applicable insolvency look-back period, the later mortgage counts as a fresh transfer.

issues.legal_issue: A statutory look-back period measured from the insolvency commencement date does not make the avoidance provision retrospective merely because it reaches transactions made before the provision came into force.
material_facts: The avoidance provisions were in force when the insolvency process and the avoidance application were pursued.
The statutory period for identifying relevant preferences was measured backwards from the insolvency commencement date and therefore included some earlier transactions.
issues.conclusion: The look-back period did not render Section 43 retrospective; the Court rejected the challenge to its operation on that basis.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 1(3) and 43(4) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code provide for the commencement of provisions and the period used to identify relevant preferences. A look-back period is an element of an operative avoidance scheme, not the imposition of a new liability merely because it covers earlier transactions. The Court distinguished Purbanchal Cables & Conductors Pvt. Ltd. v. Assam State Electricity Board, which concerned a statute imposing a new liability.

predicates.insolvency_avoidance_provision_in_force: The avoidance provision was in force when the insolvency proceeding and application for relief were pursued.
predicates.lookback_period_reaches_transactions_bef: The period for identifying reviewable transactions extends to transactions made before the avoidance provision came into force.

issues.definition: When an avoidance provision is in force and its look-back period reaches earlier transactions, that reach alone does not make the provision retrospective.

issues.legal_issue: A mortgagee holding only security over a corporate debtor’s property for debt owed by a third party is not the debtor’s financial creditor unless the debtor owes that mortgagee a financial debt.
material_facts: The lenders advanced loans to the holding company, not to the corporate debtor.
The corporate debtor mortgaged its property as collateral for the holding company’s debt.

The lenders did not disburse funds to the corporate debtor against consideration for the time value of money, and the mortgage did not make the debtor a guarantor or indemnifier for repayment of that debt.
The lenders claimed recognition as financial creditors of the corporate debtor in its insolvency process based on the mortgages.
issues.conclusion: The mortgagees could be secured creditors but were not financial creditors of the corporate debtor because it owed them no financial debt.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 5(7) and 5(8) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code require a financial creditor to be owed a financial debt, whose essential feature is disbursement against consideration for the time value of money; the listed forms of debt do not dispense with that requirement. Sections 3(10), 3(11), 3(30), and 3(31) distinguish a creditor and secured creditor from a financial creditor. A mortgage can create a security interest and a debt, but does not by itself establish a financial debt owed by the mortgagor to the mortgagee. Section 5(8)(i) may cover a guarantee or indemnity in respect of specified financial debt, but the mortgages here were not such undertakings. The Court applied Swiss Ribbons Private Limited v. Union of India and Pioneer Urban, and distinguished the secured-creditor discussion in Committee of Creditors of Essar Steel India Limited v. Satish Kumar Gupta. It also held that Smt. Kusum Vallabhdas Thakkar did not determine the meaning of financial debt under the Code.

predicates.corporate_insolvency_financial_creditor_: A person sought recognition as a financial creditor in a corporate debtor’s insolvency proceeding.
predicates.creditor_received_only_third_party_colla: The claimant received security over the corporate debtor’s property for a debt owed by another person.
predicates.no_financial_disbursement_to_corporate_d: The claimant did not disburse funds to the corporate debtor against consideration for the time value of money.
predicates.no_financial_debt_owed_by_corporate_debt: The corporate debtor did not owe the claimant a financial debt, including through a qualifying guarantee or indemnity.

issues.definition: A claimant whose only connection to the debtor is collateral for another person’s debt is not the debtor’s financial creditor when the debtor received no financial disbursement and owes no financial debt.
